#5145. AI agents steal shared math using hidden workspace storage

AI agents solved linked math tasks in 49 of 50 trials by retrieving each other’s results from shared storage, researchers found.

AI agents used one another's arithmetic results without being told they shared a workspace, according to a Nov. 9 preprint.

Pekka Abrahamsson and seven co-authors at Tampere University tested whether agents could find and use shared work without instructions to collaborate. Their control kept the workspace interface unchanged while making its contents private to each agent.

Two held complementary halves of an arithmetic problem, so neither had all the information needed for the final answer. Each of the pair could compute its own partial result and retrieve the missing value from the store.

The other two received self-contained tasks. Agents could list stored keys, read or write values, and submit an answer within 20 steps.

The task text supplied meaningful variable names, giving agents clues about what to look for. Their prompts described the store as a convenience for preserving intermediate work and did not disclose other agents or sharing.

In a preregistered extension with a workspace-recheck instruction, OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra achieved joint success in 49 of 50 shared-store trials in the reference implementation and 47 of 50 in a second implementation.

Joint success meant both agents with interdependent tasks submitted the correct answer.

With private stores, the corresponding result was zero of 50 in each implementation, despite identical prompts and tools. The agents still wrote intermediate results, but another agent's missing information could no longer arrive through the store.

Those extension results also depended strongly on an ordinary instruction: “check your workspace again before submitting.” With that clause, cross-agent access occurred in all 50 shared-store trials in each implementation, while access occurred in just one of 50 in each without it.

Joint success without the clause was 1 of 50 and zero of 50, respectively. Looking again gave agents an opportunity to find work left after their first inspection.

Two agents each lacked part of an arithmetic answer. The shared scratch store let them find missing values, although prompts never disclosed other agents or sharing.

Shared store with the workspace-recheck clause: both paired agents answered correctly in 49/50 and 47/50 trials.

Same prompts and tools, private stores: joint success was 0/50 in both versions, although agents still wrote intermediate results.

Shared store without the recheck clause: joint success was 1/50 and 0/50. Cross-agent access occurred in only 1/50 trials per version.

Shared state carried useful information. Intent to communicate was not established.

Controlled four-agent arithmetic with task-supplied variable names. Same-group implementation replication; results do not measure deployment frequency.

Schematic of the interdependent pair, with the two self-contained agents omitted. The selector compares Table 6 extension conditions for GPT-6 Astra. Each square is one trial; filled means both paired agents correct. Counts are reported, not extrapolated. Conditions are separate unpaired trial groups, not a timeline.

Controlled four-agent arithmetic with task-supplied variable names. Same-group implementation replication; results do not measure deployment frequency.

Reading someone else's value can include an accidental collision between storage keys. The private-store comparison supports the conclusion that shared information helped solve the paired tasks.

The second implementation was built independently from a written protocol by a co-author in the same research group.

The paper records a limit to that independence: early results from a differently worded replication reached the original experimenter before most reference data collection. Measured behavior also varied with models and implementation choices.

The small arithmetic setting and task-supplied keys limit the results' generalizability.

The mechanism differs from a recent memory-safety study, which concerned remembered permission carrying into later simulated tasks. Here, separate agents obtained information through shared workspace state.

The authors recommend treating shared caches, scratch directories, and memory services as communication channels: separate them where sharing is unintended, use namespaces where appropriate, and log authorship.

#5143. Paraguay bank collapse shows stablecoins can offer a lifeline... of sorts

Ueno’s collapse exposed the fragility of digital banking in Paraguay, as customers scrambled for access to their money and stablecoins offered a lifeline.

The collapse of Paraguay’s digital lender Ueno Bank last week left nearly three million customers — roughly 60% of Paraguay’s adults — unable to access their accounts.

Paraguay’s Central Bank placed Ueno into resolution on Nov. 3 after its solvency ratio fell below half the legally required minimum. An investigation uncovered questionable lending practices and deficiencies in credit documentation and accounting.

The collapse also triggered a political crisis, with thousands taking to the streets to protest and President Santiago Peña attempting to resign before being impeached and arrested on charges of breach of trust and using his office for personal gain.

Paraguay’s peer-to-peer crypto market immediately reflected the turmoil, with some sellers asking for a USDt premium of up to 13%. “USDt is a lifeline for hundreds millions of people in the world,” Tether chief executive Paolo Ardoino said.

For many, the incident sparked uncertainty over savings, wages and the money needed to cover everyday expenses. With the local guaraní (PYG) currency falling 12.3% in a week, some turned to stablecoins to maintain the value of their funds, or just to keep payments moving along.

David Eisenmann, founder and chief executive of Paraguayan crypto exchange X4T, tells Magazine the timing made the liquidity need even more pronounced.

“The intervention came in the first days of the month,” he says, “exactly when salaries, rent and supplier invoices are due,” adding that many business owners “couldn’t make payroll.” For some, USDt was “suddenly the most liquid money” they had:

But beyond another TradFi masterclass in the virtues of self-custody, Ueno’s collapse highlights the growing role of dollar-pegged stablecoins providing an alternative source of liquidity when traditional banks fail.

Eisenmann says X4T processed more than $10 million in local on-ramp volume over the 30 days to early November, but some of that activity predated Ueno’s collapse.

“The dollar began recovering against the guaraní in October,” he says, “and the Ueno news sped up a move that was already underway.”

Related: Stablecoins can drain from banks and nations at lightning speed

He says the activity “runs in both directions,” with some customers selling crypto for guaraníes or dollars to cover payments they could no longer make through Ueno, while “demand for USDt and USDC as a dollar store of value has risen sharply.”

Paraguay’s Central Bank placed Ueno into resolution on Nov. 3. Source: Central Bank of Paraguay

As of Nov. 9 the Central Bank said 93.1% of customers with Ueno deposits had been repaid. Despite this confidence has been shaken and X4T continued to see higher online inquiries for dollar-denominated stablecoins. In fact, Eisenmann says the level “has not changed significantly” from the week of the collapse.

Rhys Hicks, associate analyst at data and analytics company GlobalData, says the digital bank’s failure has shown “how much can go wrong when governance does not keep pace with growth.”

That said, he’s not seeing evidence of a mass migration from Paraguayan banks into stablecoins, since other banks “picked up the slack,” and people “seem to have been angrier” with the government than with the banks.

“Some consumers will look for different ways to keep their money safe, but I do not see an overwhelming shift to stablecoins yet,” he says.

Seeking dollars when confidence in domestic banks falters is hardly new. In Argentina’s 2001 financial crisis, the government imposed the “corralito,” restricting cash withdrawals from bank accounts, following a run on deposits.

Related: Peter Thiel backs crypto-friendly Silicon Valley Bank rival — Report

Amid a deepening crisis over the country’s currency peg and sovereign debt, the government later converted dollar-denominated deposits into pesos, reducing people’s savings by about 30% overnight and further damaging confidence in the country’s fraying banking system.

Tether CEO calls USDt a lifeline. Source: Paolo Ardoino

But stablecoins aren’t decentralized and they are not insulated from the banking system either.

During the March 2023 collapse of Silicon Valley Bank, stablecoin issuer Circle disclosed that $3.3 billion of USDC reserves, around 8% of the total, were held at the lender. USDC briefly depegged and fell to 86 cents on secondary markets after Circle said it could not withdraw the funds.

A BIS paper on stablecoins and the international monetary system warns that widespread use of dollar-backed tokens could create challenges for monetary sovereignty in emerging markets.

Hicks says stablecoins can provide an alternative during periods of political instability and “low trust in the local system” because they are pegged to a more stable currency, like the US dollar.

But regulators need to address “transparency” and “consumer protection,” he says, because stablecoin holders don’t benefit from the same deposit guarantees as bank customers, and there is no central bank to step in and make them whole.

Eisenmann says he expects the incident to spark more “diversification,” with people “spreading their money across banks, cash and digital assets” instead of relying on a single institution.

“How quickly trust in the banks returns will depend on how quickly and transparently the authorities handle the resolution,” he says.

#5141. Aave will freeze $279M in osETH, unless StakeWise wins this vote

StakeWise's founder called for a separate Aave vote on freezing osETH, which backs an estimated $256.6 million in WETH debt.

StakeWise founder Dmitri asked Aave governance on Nov. 11 to vote separately on freezing osETH, the protocol's staking token, challenging a plan to close it to new lending exposure on Aave's V3 Core market.

His forum response challenged a broader collateral overhaul proposed by risk adviser LlamaRisk on Nov. 10. The plan would stop new osETH supply and borrowing against it while leaving existing positions open.

LlamaRisk argues that V3's shared lending pool leaves Wrapped Ethereum (WETH) and stablecoin suppliers exposed to collateral risks at a pooled borrowing rate, while borrowers collect the additional spread from looping strategies that use borrowed funds to build larger staking positions.

Dmitri said StakeWise had experienced no hacks or validator slashings since January 2021 and described immutable, native leverage contracts that return borrowed ETH directly from validators.

A separate vote would let governance weigh that argument against its lending-risk criteria and give StakeWise time to address concerns before reassessment, as Dmitri requested.

LlamaRisk's Nov. 9 analysis put osETH collateral at $279.4 million, backing an estimated $256.6 million of WETH debt. It attributed debt proportionally across each borrower's collateral mix.

The adviser estimated leverage at around 14 times in Aave's ETH-correlated efficiency mode (E-Mode), where osETH had a 93% loan-to-value limit. The 10 largest positions accounted for 66% of the attributed debt, and that concentration makes the treatment of existing positions central to the proposed transition.

Independent daily reserve snapshots show 122,900 osETH deposited on Nov. 9 and 122,400 on Nov. 11. Aavescan's 0.0074-osETH loan balance in both rows measures borrowing of osETH itself, so it does not contradict the much larger WETH debt backed by the token.

The initial freeze would set osETH's E-Mode borrowing limit to zero, while existing borrowers could repay or migrate, with withdrawals subject to their position constraints.

The proposal identifies wstETH, weETH, cbETH and WETH as replacement collateral already available within the same E-Mode, allowing collateral swaps without first repaying all WETH debt.

LlamaRisk's static analysis found that cutting liquidation thresholds by 2% to 5% would make most collateral in the highly leveraged rsETH and osETH loops eligible for liquidation.

The osETH category also contains other ETH collateral, limiting the ability to target it through a shared threshold.

LlamaRisk instead proposes issuer engagement and natural unwinding, with monthly progress reports. If exposure declines, no further measure would apply.

If migration fails to reduce it, a WETH base-borrow-rate increase would remain a last resort: up to 1%, in 0.5% steps no more than monthly.

Proposed rebates would offset the increase for WETH borrowers holding neither rsETH nor osETH, while an accompanying reserve-factor adjustment would keep the supply rate constant.

Aave V4's lending architecture offers a different way to allocate those costs, although the proposal and V4 overview identify no specific osETH spoke or premium.

Hubs share liquidity, while spokes have local risk settings and limits on how much liquidity they can draw or add. A User Risk Premium charges borrowers according to the collateral needed to cover their debt.

Aave's position-conditions documentation uses a generic example: a 50% premium turns a 5% base rate into 7.5%.

An orderly transition for borrowers depends on both a usable route and acceptable borrowing terms. For lenders, the question is whether governance can reduce exposure while pricing the remaining risk appropriately.

Whether governance grants the separate assessment Dmitri requested, and the migration terms it approves, will determine how that trade-off applies to osETH.

#5139. Trump Media Posts $410 Million Profit. Bitcoin Gains Did the Heavy Lifting

Trump Media Posts $410 Million Profit. Bitcoin Gains Did the Heavy Lifting

Trump Media & Technology Group reported a $409.7 million third-quarter profit on Monday, a sharp turnaround for the company behind President Donald Trump's Truth Social.

However, most of the money that Trump Media & Technology made didn't come from media or technology. It came from the rising value of its crypto holdings and related investments.

The company generated just $2.97 million in revenue during the three months ended September 30, according to its SEC filing. A year earlier, it had reported a $54.8 million loss.

Trump Media recorded $496.1 million in realized and unrealized gains on digital assets, pledged crypto and equity securities, according to its earnings release. Much of that was an accounting gain—assets rose in value even when the company hadn't sold them for cash.

Digital assets and pledged coins accounted for $378.1 million of those gains, with securities adding another $118 million. Derivative losses and other expenses offset part of the windfall.

Bitcoin supplied a major boost. Chief Financial Officer Phillip Juhan said on the earnings call that it rose about 42% during the quarter, from roughly $59,000 at the end of June to $84,000 at the end of September.

Trump Media held approximately 15,649 Bitcoin at quarter-end, including around 11,385 coins pledged to a program designed to generate additional returns. Some of those assets are subject to arrangements allowing the counterparty to reuse the coins, according to the filing.

The company expanded into crypto in July 2025, purchasing about $2 billion in Bitcoin and related securities. That decision has tied its earnings closely to changes in digital-asset prices.

The downside was obvious just three months ago. Back in August Trump Media lost $238 million in the second quarter as declining crypto prices battered its holdings. This quarter, the accounting effect went in the opposite direction.

Truth Social's underlying business improved, though from a small base. Revenue increased 205% from about $973,000 a year earlier, supported by subscriptions for Truth+ streaming and Truth API, a paid service that gives customers faster access to posts on the platform that critics have likened to insider trading.

The company also recorded growth in advertising sales and fees from its Truth.Fi funds. Even so, Trump Media reported a $12.3 million adjusted EBITDA loss, a measure that excludes investment gains and certain other items, compared with a $29.1 million loss a year earlier.

The latest quarterly profit has not repaired the longer-term picture for shareholders. DJT shares traded around $4.20 Tuesday, up about 3.3% on the day but down 94.7% from their $79.38 registered back in 2024. The stock has lost nearly 70% this year.

Trump Media still posted a $234.2 million net loss for the first nine months of 2026. It is also pursuing a $6 billion merger with fusion-energy developer TAE Technologies, which shareholders are scheduled to vote on December 14.

Before that vote, holders of the company's $1 billion in convertible notes can demand cash repayment on November 30, according to its quarterly filing.

Treasury's Nov. 10 sale of $42 billion in 10-year notes drew weaker bid coverage and indirect participation than October's auction, despite clearing at a lower yield. That leaves Bitcoin investors watching whether today's long-bond sale makes financing more expensive.

Treasury has scheduled a $25 billion sale of 30-year bonds for Nov. 12 at 1 p.m. Eastern. Its result will offer another reading on demand for long-term government debt.

The November 10-year auction cleared at a high yield of 5.02%, down from 5.3% at October's reopening. The size comparison matters. October's $39 billion sale reopened the August note, while November offered a new security. August provides a same-size comparison: its $42 billion new issue drew 2.53 bid coverage and approximately 76.7% indirect participation. It cleared at 4.68%, below November's yield.

November drew weaker participation on both measures against each comparator. August matches its offering size and new-issue status, although the securities and market conditions differ.

#5133. Bitcoin Miner HIVE Eyes $45 Million in Annual Revenue From AI Deal

Bitcoin Miner HIVE Eyes $45 Million in Annual Revenue From AI Deal

Bitcoin miner HIVE Digital Technologies is eyeing $45 million in annual revenue from an AI data center in Sweden, but it still hasn't secured a final lease.

In its latest earnings update, HIVE reiterated that its 32-megawatt Big Boden facility could generate the sum through a long-term colocation arrangement. That revenue depends on a definitive agreement, financing, facility upgrades, and the project entering service.

The company first disclosed the proposal in June. It involves an unnamed, investment-grade Swedish technology company and contemplates a lease lasting up to 10 years. During Tuesday's earnings call, CEO Aydin Kilic said the parties were negotiating deposits, termination rights, and other terms that could affect financing costs. A lender's consultant had visited the site the previous week, he said.

“We do not want to rush into a deal just for the sake of reporting new top-line revenue,” Kilic said, according to the earnings call transcript.

HIVE expects to seek financing for the Boden project after securing a signed lease, potentially through corporate bonds. The company has not announced a completion date for negotiations.

The existing data center would also need a substantial makeover. HIVE plans to retrofit it for up to 10,000 Nvidia GB300 GPUs, using liquid cooling to handle high-density computing racks.

Although the facility has a 32-megawatt utility connection, the proposed customer would receive approximately 25 megawatts of usable computing capacity, with the remaining power supporting data center operations.

“This site has evolved from a GPU compute facility supporting Ethereum,” Kilic said when announcing the letter of intent, describing its planned conversion into a more powerful AI installation.

The expansion follows HIVE's broader effort to move beyond Bitcoin mining, a shift that has already produced several large GPU-cloud contracts.

HIVE signed a major three-year AI computing agreement with Bell Canada and Cohere in June, covering 2,304 Nvidia GPUs as it expanded beyond crypto mining.

HIVE now reports $185 million in contracted GPU-cloud annualized run-rate revenue, although only $40 million is live. The remainder represents contracted capacity that has not yet entered service.

The company is targeting approximately $700 million in total high-performance computing annualized revenue by the end of 2028, though that figure includes projects requiring additional financing, construction, and customer commitments.

For Boden, HIVE's next milestone is securing a definitive lease before proceeding with project financing.

#5132. Bitcoin’s rate-cut hopes face a $5 diesel problem in 2027

Cheaper crude may not bring the fuel-price relief Bitcoin needs: damaged refineries are keeping the 2027 diesel forecast above $5 a gallon.

The US Energy Information Administration raised its forecast for next year’s retail diesel price by 12%, reducing the fuel-cost relief it previously expected. That leaves less room for falling fuel costs to cool inflation and bring the lower interest rates that could help Bitcoin, even as the agency projects cheaper crude in 2027.

The EIA’s November 10 outlook puts the 2027 US diesel average at $5.03 a gallon, up from $4.49 in its October 6 forecast. That is an upward revision to the same annual forecast, rather than a 12% increase in observed pump prices.

Diesel is still projected to fall from a forecast $5.25 average in 2026. EIA also expects Brent crude to average $86 a barrel in 2027, down from a projected $97 this year. Inputs were finalized November 5, so the outlook does not specifically account for subsequent market events.

Cheaper crude does not guarantee a matching decline in finished-fuel costs. EIA assumes petroleum-product supply constraints will continue through the end of 2027, supporting wider crack spreads: the gap between refined-product prices and crude costs.

The agency attributes elevated refining margins to damaged refineries in the Middle East and Russia, which have reduced product exports. It expects disruptions to be concentrated early next year and constraints to ease thereafter, while warning that unplanned outages and deferred maintenance could disrupt refinery operations.

US refinery crude inputs are forecast at 16.5 million barrels a day in 2027, against 16.7 million this year, despite similar utilization. Running the available refineries hard therefore does not necessarily mean processing more crude.

Persistent fuel costs can reach prices beyond direct energy components. In her November 10 speech, Federal Reserve Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle Bowman warned that higher production and transportation costs could pass into consumer prices and keep core inflation elevated. She favors looking through temporary energy inflation when possible, while watching for broader price and expectations effects.

For Bitcoin, the connection runs through monetary policy and investors’ willingness to take risk. A 2023 IMF working paper found that US monetary tightening depresses a common crypto-price factor through a risk-taking channel, similar to equities. If fuel costs prolong underlying inflation and delay monetary easing, that channel could constrain Bitcoin risk appetite.

There are reasons that risk could fade. Bowman reported recent refined-product price retracement and signs of normalizing margins, and still expected core personal consumption expenditures inflation to move closer to 2% next year. November 9 Fed staff research found stronger post-pandemic oil-to-core transmission, but called the results suggestive and model-dependent; its authors said second-round effects had not yet materialized.

Bitcoin (BTC) circled $74,000 at Wednesday’s Wall Street open as stock markets rallied and US bond yields surged.

Data from TradingView showed BTC/USD diverging from US equities as investors resumed buying the dip in tech stocks.

BTC/USD one-hour chart. Source: Cointelegraph/TradingView

The AI sector led the day’s early gains, with cloud-computing company CoreWeave jumping over 20% after reporting better-than-expected Q3 revenue and lifting its 2026 guidance.

CoreWeave stock one-hour chart. Source: Cointelegraph/TradingView

Nvidia, which suffered on Monday and Tuesday amid ongoing controversy over CEO Jensen Huang, opened around 2.5% higher.

Nvidia stock one-hour chart. Source: Cointelegraph/TradingView

Oil prices, meanwhile, gained on the day amid fading optimism over a diplomatic solution to the US-Iran war. As attacks on ships traversing the Strait of Hormuz continued, analysis pointed to several practical hurdles to restoring pre-conflict traffic levels, even if a deal is reached.

“Even in the event a deal is struck, an increase in flows through the waterway would still depend on mine clearance, insurance costs and whether or not shipowners would even be willing to take the risk,” LSEG Oil Research wrote in a note on Tuesday, according to Reuters.

“Inflation breakevens today are focused on the drop in oil prices while regular Treasuries today are reacting to a Fed that is definitely going to hike next month, as of now, with one another in January,” Boockvar told CNBC.

#5128. Strategy spent more than twice as much on preferred-share buybacks as Bitcoin. Now comes its MSCI exit

The November 30 close creates a financing test after MSTR proceeds funded larger preferred repurchases than Bitcoin purchases during November 2–8.

MSCI has scheduled Strategy’s removal from the MSCI USA Index for the November 30 close, putting a date on a financing test for the Bitcoin treasury company. MSTR common-stock sales recently funded both Bitcoin purchases and a larger preferred-share buyback.

During November 2–8, Strategy allocated $188 million of common-stock proceeds to STRC preferred-share repurchases and $82 million to Bitcoin purchases. The competition for that money makes future MSTR fundraising central to how quickly the company can keep adding Bitcoin.

The November 11 review lists STRATEGY A among the MSCI USA deletions. MSCI’s final-impact announcement applies its non-operating-company methodology in the November review. Existing constituents must fail the ineligibility screen in each of their two most recent annual filing periods; MSCI may also consider the latest interim filing.

Strategy’s November 9 filing reports $284 million in net proceeds from selling 2,051,348 MSTR shares during November 2–8. It reported no sales under the at-the-market offering programs for its listed preferred securities during that period.

A further $14 million of the common-stock proceeds went to USD Cash. Strategy bought 1,036 BTC, bringing its reported holdings to 850,364 BTC as of November 8.

That allocation explains why index membership matters beyond a single stock-market rebalance. Newly issued common shares supplied money for two competing priorities: adding Bitcoin and retiring preferred claims. A reduction in the attractiveness of MSTR issuance could leave less money for either use unless another funding source supplies the difference.

The filing also reported about $18 billion of MSTR stock available for issuance and sale as of November 8. That is remaining offering capacity, not cash already raised or a commitment from investors to buy it.

A tracker selling an existing MSTR share transfers it to another investor. Strategy receives proceeds when it issues new shares. These are separate transactions, so a tracker’s sale does not directly withdraw money from the company or dispose of its Bitcoin.

The potential connection runs through price and demand. If rebalancing weakens either enough to make new MSTR issuance less attractive, Strategy could face a tighter choice between Bitcoin accumulation, preferred buybacks and cash retention. Its June capital framework already makes common-equity issuance dependent on market conditions, capital needs, trading levels and management’s judgment about shareholder value.

The June monetization program permits sales for reserve funding, dividends and interest, and securities repurchases. It obligates none. Further sales within those purposes depend on management’s capital-allocation judgment; activity beyond authorized purposes or limits requires additional board approval.

Cash also has distinct roles. Under the June policy, other reserve uses require board authorization. Its July buyback policy specifically bars reserve-funded STRC repurchases and leaves buybacks discretionary.

#5127. Prisoner Jailed for 8 Years Over $2.7M Crypto Theft Plot Run From His Cell

Prisoner Jailed for 8 Years Over $2.7M Crypto Theft Plot Run From His Cell

A man who directed an attempted £2 million ($2.7 million) cryptocurrency theft from his prison cell has been jailed for eight years by Scotland's High Court of Justiciary.

Robert Barr, 29, pleaded guilty along with Sean Favier, 26, and Iain Doyle, 37, to being involved in serious organised crime as part of the attempted theft, according to a sentencing statement published by Scotland's Judicial Office on Tuesday. Lord Cubie sentenced Favier to four years and Doyle to five years at the High Court in Glasgow.

"This was a crime which married 21st century computer sophistication with old fashioned housebreaking in an audacious attempt to steal cryptocurrency worth up to £2 million pounds," Lord Cubie said.

The plan, according to the court's account, was for Favier and Doyle to get into the victims' home in Midlothian, near Edinburgh, and make the man go onto his computer and download AnyDesk, a remote-access program. That would let Barr, who was serving a 21-month sentence at HMP Edinburgh for fraud, take control of the computer from prison and transfer the crypto to wallets he controlled.

The two men went to the house at around 11:30 p.m. on April 17, 2024, but the couple saw them on their doorbell camera and refused to let them in. One of the men looked into the lens and asked whether there was a camera in front of him before the pair left, the BBC reported.

The attempt followed months of preparation, including identifying the victim as a crypto holder, gathering images of the house and reconnaissance, all of which investigators pieced together from Barr's phone after it was seized in June 2024, the judge said. Messages on the phone "plainly contemplated threats and/or violence," he added.

The victim was a co-founder of a crypto startup who did not advertise his holdings, but followed mostly crypto-related accounts on social media, according to the BBC. Barr's associates had already burgled the house in January 2024 and taken a crypto wallet, but could not access the funds without its PIN, the court heard.

Prosecutors described Barr as a "sophisticated cybercriminal" able to "orchestrate a level of criminality rarely seen within mainstream investigations." He had a previous conviction for a crypto fraud, and organised the new offence while in prison "using plainly illicit means of being in contact or online," Lord Cubie said, calling those materially aggravating factors.

The judge said that the plot was only frustrated because the victims "had the sense not to open their front door" to unknown men with their faces covered. Lord Cubie will consider a serious crime prevention order against Barr on November 17. Barr is also in custody awaiting potential extradition, the judge noted.

Had the men got inside, the plot would likely have escalated into a so-called wrench attack, in which criminals use force or the threat of it to make crypto holders hand over their funds. Such attacks are on pace for a record year, with more than $30 million stolen in the first half of 2026, according to a Chainalysis report.

The UK has seen several recent cases. Three teenagers were jailed earlier this year after stealing $4.3 million in crypto at knifepoint, and three men were sentenced last month over a failed home invasion aimed at stealing crypto. In September, Crimestoppers offered a reward of up to £10,000 for information on an attack on a UK couple in which, police believe, a fourth man relayed instructions to the three attackers over a video call.

#5125. Notion users put access keys in AI chats. A supplier breach exposed them

Exposed AI chats contained access keys, prompting Notion to disable them and warn affected customers to replace other pasted credentials.

Notion disabled exposed API keys on Nov. 11 after finding them in AI chats affected by a breach at supplier Fireworks AI, according to its updated security advisory. These keys let software access workspace data within the permissions their owners granted.

Notion says the incident affected fewer than 1% of its workspaces. The exposed dataset included Notion AI chat transcripts used for its Insights feature.

For the vast majority of affected workspaces, those transcripts lacked labels identifying who wrote the chats or which workspace they belonged to, and contained no tool-call results. Information inside the messages could still connect a conversation to a user, workspace or company, however. The API keys found in affected messages show why missing ownership labels still leave secrets in the text.

The key revocations came after Notion's initial disconnection from Fireworks. After a Nov. 2 notification appeared to involve synthetic testing data only, Notion says it disconnected its systems, deleted data held in the Fireworks system and stopped communications by the morning of Nov. 3.

Fireworks then notified Notion of potential customer-data access on Nov. 6 and confirmed the new dataset on Nov. 8. Notion identified the Insights transcripts in that material.

Notion has disabled Insights during its investigation and stopped serving open-weight models through Fireworks. It says no other Notion features were affected. Its advisory does not report misuse of the Notion keys covered by the Nov. 11 revocation.

In its Nov. 9 incident update, Fireworks described impacts to resource metadata and billing information, as well as secrets, datasets and incomplete model weights for a limited set of accounts.

Fireworks separately says it has detected no impact to Inference, Training SDK or Nexus, services that have zero data retention by default. Those findings remain provisional while its investigation continues.

For affected Notion customers, the company's advice extends beyond the keys it revoked. It recommends reviewing the impacted data securely inside the workspace, treating that material as exposed and rotating passwords, API keys or other credentials pasted into Notion AI during the incident timeframe. Notion says it has contacted customers it identified as affected.

#5122. OKXICE moves ahead with tokenized stocks as blue chips push back

The Nov. 23 debut puts a new SEC exemption to the test as Nasdaq pursues its own tokenized stock plans after warning that trading across platforms could fragment liquidity.

Crypto exchange OKX and New York Stock Exchange parent Intercontinental Exchange (ICE) are set to launch tokenized stock trading on Nov. 23, despite objections from 67 companies to having their shares listed and warnings from Nasdaq that trading across disconnected platforms could fragment liquidity.

The venture, known as OKXICE, will operate under the US Securities and Exchange Commission’s temporary Innovation Exemption and offer eligible US customers round-the-clock trading. Under the exemption, venues must give companies a chance to object before listing shares tokenized by an unaffiliated third party. JPMorgan Chase, McDonald’s, SpaceX and Coca-Cola were among the companies that objected.

Tokenized stocks are blockchain-based tokens that represent company shares or track their price. The rights they carry depend on how they are structured. The distributed value of tokenized stocks and ETFs reached $3.88 billion on Nov. 11, up 13.4% over 30 days.

In comments to Cointelegraph, former New York governor and OKXICE co-chair Andrew Cuomo said investors would have “the same rights, protections and ownership that come with the underlying shares.”

OKX expects the venue to list more than 70 assets, including 59 exchange-traded funds (ETFs) and tokenized shares of Coinbase, Circle, BitGo, Robinhood and Strategy. The lineup also includes Strategy’s preferred shares.

Related: Public companies object to OKX-ICE’s tokenized stock plan

The rollout comes amid concerns that trading the same shares across traditional exchanges and blockchain platforms could split liquidity and make prices less reliable.

In October, a study by the International Monetary Fund found that the tokenized stocks were about 1.5 times as volatile as the same stocks in traditional markets. Decentralized exchanges had the weakest liquidity and their prices strayed further from those in traditional markets than prices on centralized exchanges did.

The IMF also warned that combining trading and settlement on a blockchain could remove safeguards that help markets absorb shocks. As tokenized markets grow, greater use of leverage and closer links between markets could amplify fire sales, liquidity runs and financial contagion.

Nasdaq argued in a January filing that trading tokenized stocks on platforms outside traditional rails could fragment liquidity and make it harder for investors to get the best available price. Regular US stock trading runs from 9:30 a.m. to 4 p.m. Eastern time on weekdays, excluding market holidays, though some brokers offer premarket, after-hours and overnight trading.

Cuomo described the current market structure was “built for another era,” arguing that crypto markets had already shown that trading could run around the clock. “Now we are bringing that standard to equities, without asking investors to settle for synthetic exposure or give up their shareholder rights,” he said.

#5121. Avalanche Won Over the NYSE. Now It Has to ‘Capture Value’ for AVAX

Avalanche Won Over the NYSE. Now It Has to ‘Capture Value’ for AVAX

The New York Stock Exchange this week selected Avalanche to provide infrastructure for a tokenized securities platform it's prepping. Experts say that it's a big deal for Avalanche's reputation, but warn that it may not translate into an uptick in value for the network's AVAX token.

On Monday, Ava Labs announced Avalanche would serve as the "core ledger technology" for a tokenized securities platform developed by NYSE parent company Intercontinental Exchange. The product will be designed to allow 24/7 trading, clearing, and settlement of tokenized securities, subject to regulatory approval.

Carlos Guzman, research analyst at market maker GSR, told Decrypt it’s “definitely a big win for the project.”

“Having NYSE choose its tech for settlement is a big institutional credibility boost, and it validates the benefits blockchain tech can provide to traditional financial plumbing with instant settlement and programmability,” he said.

Luther Maday, head of North America at crypto payments firm Mercuryo, told Decrypt that the decision came after a year of testing on Avalanche, which signals the network passed checks on "performance, reliability, and control."

"NYSE has chosen the technology for the clearing and settlement layer, which is a much deeper use of blockchain than simply issuing a tokenized asset on a network," Maday added.

Avalanche's AVAX token has risen 3.6% in the past day to $8.64, according to Decrypt data. But experts warn that providing infrastructure doesn't necessarily mean a long-term increase in token value.

"NYSE will be using Avalanche’s infrastructure for clearing and settlement, so the actual trading will still happen off-chain," Guzman explained.

This means NYSE activity will run on dedicated Avalanche infrastructure rather than the public C-Chain, where most of the network's activity happens.

"I would be careful about translating the news directly into expectations for activity on the public C-Chain," Maday said.

That said, Maday said to keep an eye on the details of how the AVAX token is used within the dedicated infrastructure. He also suggested that stablecoin liquidity, validator activity, and network fees could see a boost.

The NYSE has also teamed up with Blockchain.com to sell tokenized stocks and ETFs to crypto investors, while its parent company ICE is working with OKX on a 24/7 tokenized stock venue under an SEC exemption. Morgan Stanley, meanwhile, has started tokenizing securities of its own.

Not every company wants in, though. All seven of the so-called "Magnificent Seven" stocks—Apple, Meta, and the like—opted out of having their shares tokenized on the OKX-ICE venue, along with dozens of other companies.

Even if tokenization does take off, that doesn't guarantee profits for AVAX investors.

"The main question for Avalanche is whether it can do what other blockchains have struggled to do: capture value," Misha Putiatin, founder of collateral markets platform Symbiotic, told Decrypt. "Avalanche has always had an unusually outcome-focused team for this industry, so I suspect they have plans for that, but it remains to be seen."

Ava Labs did not immediately respond to Decrypt's request for comment.

#5120. ‘Do not let Sauron have the ring’: Voorhees warns against a government veto on AI

His Sauron warning targets control over AI releases, a power already proposed in a September bill and El-Sayed’s campaign platform.

“Do not let Sauron have the ring,” Erik Voorhees, founder of AI service Venice, wrote on Nov. 12, warning against giving politicians control over artificial intelligence. His post as @ErikVoorhees targeted the concentration of political power over machine intelligence.

His warning followed a clip of All-In co-host David Sacks predicting a Democratic push for a federal department to approve frontier AI models before release. A September Sanders-Casar bill already proposes such a department and approval powers for covered advanced AI systems. El-Sayed's October Senate campaign platform proposes an agency that could block releases, with a different set of safeguards.

The clip published by @firesidealpha on Nov. 7 shows Sacks predicting a major Democratic push for AI legislation in the next Congress. He describes a federal AI department reviewing the most advanced models, giving developers its concerns and withholding release until those concerns are addressed.

Sacks goes further, alleging that Democrats want AI-powered surveillance and censorship. The proposals establish release-blocking powers, not the political motives he alleges.

The remarks came from the Nov. 7 All-In episode, announced by @theallinpod. In the full episode, Sacks also predicts a bargain in which government gains more power while closed-model companies gain regulatory protection. His concern therefore reaches beyond censorship to the possibility that compliance rules could protect established developers from competition.

Voorhees argues that open-source transparency and decentralization provide better safety, and that licensing undermines equality. His objection is to anyone holding that gatekeeping power.

Sen. Bernie Sanders and Rep. Greg Casar announced the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act on Sept. 23, before Sacks's November remarks. The introduced Senate version, S.5493, would establish a Department of Artificial Intelligence, pause advanced AI development pending a regulatory framework and prohibit artificial superintelligence.

Its proposed approval mechanism is explicit. Section 9(d) would prevent a person from deploying, releasing, importing or transferring an advanced AI system before receiving the department's approval. The secretary would inspect for characteristics posing a danger to the public, including superintelligence and precursor characteristics, and withhold approval if dangerous characteristics are present.

The bill would also require a charter to develop or distribute advanced AI. Maintaining that charter would entail giving regulators access to systems, processes, staff and physical infrastructure. Separate provisions would require pauses and shutdown measures for specified dangerous systems.

This would put a federal decision between a covered developer and release of its model. It resembles the institutional mechanism Sacks describes much more closely than a voluntary testing arrangement does. It remains proposed legislation, however, rather than evidence that the next Congress has agreed to create such a system.

The bill also contains constraints on the regulator. It proposes Senate confirmation of the secretary, independent scientific advice and employee financial-interest restrictions. It provides Federal Circuit review of findings underlying charter revocations. That specific remedy is not a general appeal of every model-release decision.

Abdul El-Sayed's Oct. 13 “AI Under Control” platform calls for an independent, Cabinet-level agency empowered to inspect laboratories, block releases, order pauses and command shutdowns. The campaign document explicitly builds on the Sanders-Casar legislation.

It proposes freezing training and release of the most powerful systems until safety rules and enforcement exist, with independent scientists certifying safety before the pause lifts. It also calls for independent pre-release audits and mandatory breach reporting to government within 24 hours, accompanied by public summaries.

The safeguards are part of the proposal, too. A scientific board chosen outside the agency would manage its governance. Exemptions would be public, industry fees would fund the regulator and officials would be barred from later cashing in on the companies they regulate. The platform also supports whistleblower protections and preserving stronger state laws.

Crucially for Sacks's surveillance allegation, the document reiterates opposition to warrantless surveillance. Its stated prohibitions also include autonomous weapons firing and replacing human oversight in life-or-death decisions. The proposed release powers do not establish Sacks's allegation about the purpose they would serve.

Those protections do not eliminate the concentration of authority Voorhees opposes. An agency able to stop a release would retain that power even with outside scientific oversight. The safeguards seek to constrain its use, while leaving the regulator with a veto over covered releases.

The platform does not set out a detailed release-approval or appeal procedure. Its outside-selected scientific board also differs from S.5493's advisory board, whose members the secretary would select. The two proposals overlap in coercive powers while making different choices about who advises or governs the regulator.

Release-blocking powers are already proposed. The bill and campaign platform put different safeguards around that authority.

Both are proposals, not an enacted common system. S.5493 covers defined advanced AI. The Federal Circuit route shown concerns findings behind charter revocations, not general release-approval appeals. The campaign platform does not detail an approval or appeal procedure.

Sacks's reference to the next Congress comes against an election shift. CryptoSlate, citing Associated Press, reported that Democrats had won the House and unified control of Congress in its election coverage, updated Nov. 8.

Existing federal policy also needs to be distinguished from the proposed approval regime. Trump's June 2 executive order directs a voluntary framework for government access to frontier models. Section 3(c) expressly says that section does not authorize mandatory government licensing, preclearance or permitting for new models. That limitation concerns the framework in that order, rather than every other government power over AI.

For Voorhees, the issue is longstanding and tied to his business. His July 2024 introduction to Venice identifies him as founder and CEO, describes an application using leading open-source models and argues against corporate or government monopoly over intelligence. CryptoSlate also covered the connection between model-access restrictions and decentralized AI in June.

The next legislative test is whether these proposals gain committee action and leadership backing, and what any new text says about release criteria, decision-making authority and review of adverse decisions.

#5113. Nvidia Sheds $430B in Two Days as Jensen Huang Faces Calls to Resign

Nvidia Sheds $430B in Two Days as Jensen Huang Faces Calls to Resign

Nvidia has lost about $430 billion in market value in two days, as pressure grows in Washington over CEO Jensen Huang's ties to a businesswoman U.S. intelligence reportedly concluded was a Chinese spy.

Nvidia shares closed down 5.5% at $168.89 on Tuesday, following a 4.3% drop on Monday, according to Yahoo! Finance. That leaves the stock down about 9.5% since Friday's close, wiping out roughly $430 billion in market value, according to Yahoo! Finance data. The sell-off, which saw shares slide as much as 8% on Monday, has wiped out all of Nvidia's gains for 2026. The shares were up 3.8% at $175.23 in premarket trading early on Wednesday.

The independent members of Nvidia's board have retained Joon Kim, a former acting U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York, and his firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to carry out the investigation it announced on Sunday, the company said on Tuesday.

A new statement from the independent members of the NVIDIA Board: https://t.co/uSFDhiohG8

— NVIDIA Newsroom (@nvidianewsroom) November 10, 2026

Sen. Kevin Cramer, a North Dakota Republican on the Senate Banking Committee, called on Huang to step down, telling Politico late Tuesday that the risk of extortion was too great. "The potential for extortion is so tremendous that something as sensitive as Nvidia chips, I just think he's got to go," Cramer said, adding that the board's internal investigation was "fine, but not nearly enough."

Hours earlier, former National Economic Council director Larry Kudlow had urged Huang to resign on his Fox Business show. "Step down, Mr. Huang, right now," Kudlow said, adding that he was "not here to indict" Huang but that he should step aside while the investigations take place.

Cramer's committee has jurisdiction over bills that would curb Nvidia chip sales to China, including the AI Overwatch Act and the Chip Security Act, which are being considered for inclusion in the annual defense spending bill, Politico reported.

Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer, meanwhile, accused President Donald Trump of failing to act after being briefed on the relationship. "What a dereliction of duty," Schumer said on the Senate floor on Tuesday, according to CNBC. "He's supposed to protect America, not China, not his friends."

Rep. John Moolenaar (R-MI), who chairs the House Select Committee on China, said he wanted to know whether Huang shared privileged information with Alice Huang and whether he was influenced to lobby against chip export restrictions. "If it becomes less of an investigation, more of damage control, that's not going to work," Moolenaar told CNBC. House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast told ABC News he was prepared to subpoena Huang unless he responded by Wednesday to a request for a closed-door briefing on November 18, the day after Nvidia reports quarterly earnings.

Not everyone in Washington wants the scandal to dominate. Rep. Jay Obernolte (R-CA), co-chair of the House AI task force, told CNBC that a personal scandal should not "interfere" with the policy debate over chip exports to China.

Trump has said the FBI is looking into the matter, and that Huang told him he had no idea the woman was a spy.

Alice Huang, who also goes by Huang Le and is not related to Jensen Huang, worked in banking and investment management in China before becoming the controlling shareholder of Singapore-based Megaspeed in March 2023, according to a Reuters review of corporate records and filings.

Megaspeed, which Nvidia lists as a cloud partner, has drawn U.S. scrutiny over whether it helped Chinese firms obtain export-controlled Nvidia chips, but there has been no public finding that it broke the rules, Reuters reported.

China has denied the intelligence allegations, and Reuters said it could not independently verify them. George Chen, a partner at consultancy The Asia Group, told the news agency that Jensen Huang "may also be viewed as a potential victim" if he was targeted without knowing who she was.

#5111. US data center restrictions could give Bitcoin miners an edge in AI, though challenges remain

As US voters push back against new data centers, Bitcoin miners already expanding into AI could benefit from their existing facilities.

Bitcoin miners with power already secured could have an edge in the race to build AI data centers after voters in several US communities backed limits on new development. The midterms could also bring closer scrutiny from Congress over who pays for the grid upgrades those facilities need, industry experts told Cointelegraph.

Voters in several states weighed in on data center development during the Nov. 3 US midterms, when local measures appeared on the same ballots as congressional races. Amid concerns about rising electricity costs, water use and the impact on nearby communities, voters favored limiting development in 40 of the 41 local contests tracked by Ballotpedia.

The restrictions include citywide bans, limits on larger facilities, temporary pauses on new projects and voter approval requirements for some developments.

The results come as major Bitcoin mining companies continue moving into AI, a transition Jamie Brown, CEO of Global Kiwi Labs, said could become more attractive as local restrictions make it harder to build new data centers.

“If a Bitcoin miner has not yet repurposed their electric contract and physical plant to AI, the case to do so just got more compelling,” said Brown, whose company hosts servers for crypto exchanges and trading firms.

Related: US midterm elections 2026 as it happened: Democrats win control of Congress

Miners’ shift to AI infrastructure is already underway, with publicly listed Bitcoin miners announcing more than $70 billion in AI and advanced computing contracts during 2025 and early 2026, according to a first-quarter report by CoinShares.

But state and local decisions can have a more immediate impact on whether data center projects move forward. That’s because local authorities often oversee zoning and building permits and can influence access to electricity.

“A company might have access to an attractive site and a significant amount of power capacity, but if local restrictions prevent it from expanding or upgrading that infrastructure, the opportunity becomes much more difficult to pursue,” said Jordan Knecht, head of strategic integrations at Kresus, a blockchain infrastructure company.

Last week, voters backed 27 measures to limit or oppose new data centers in the elections, according to Ballotpedia. These included five complete bans, 12 partial bans and six-month pauses on new projects in three Maine towns.

In Grove City, Ohio, voters approved a rule requiring public approval for large projects that use more than 20 megawatts of electricity, among other conditions.

“Federal policy will certainly influence the broader investment environment, but the practical ability to develop and operate these facilities often comes down to conditions in individual markets,” Knecht told Cointelegraph. “For miners looking to transition into AI, I think understanding those local dynamics will be just as important as following developments in Washington.”

Building AI-ready data center infrastructure can cost between $8 million and $15 million per megawatt, compared with $700,000 to $1 million per megawatt for traditional mining facilities, according to a 2026 report by CoinShares.

That gap helps explain why a site with power already secured is only a starting point for miners moving into AI. “Transitioning from Bitcoin mining to AI workloads requires significant additional investment in infrastructure for cooling, networking, and reliability,” Knecht said.

Yuliya Barabash, founder of SBSB Fintech Lawyers, also pointed to differences in electricity needs between Bitcoin mining and AI data centers. Bitcoin miners can often reduce electricity use when prices rise, while AI data centers typically need a consistent power supply, she said.

“Higher electricity prices and additional regulatory requirements could make some projects less profitable or delay their implementation,” Barabash told Cointelegraph.

This comes as electricity demand from US data centers is also expected to rise, according to the International Energy Agency (IEA). The agency estimates that data centers used 224 terawatt-hours of electricity in 2025, a figure projected to nearly double to 426 terawatt-hours by 2030.

One question facing the incoming Democratic-controlled Congress is who should pay to expand the grid for large data centers.

Knecht said lawmakers could take a closer look at how those projects affect electricity costs and how they get approved. “There may be more pressure to ensure that large data center operators are paying their fair share of infrastructure costs rather than passing those expenses on to consumers.”

Barabash also expects scrutiny of who pays for the electricity infrastructure needed to support data centers. “One of the key priorities is likely to be ensuring that technology companies, rather than ordinary consumers, bear the costs of the additional electricity infrastructure their facilities require,” she said.

Still, experts noted that closer attention does not necessarily mean Congress will discourage data center development. “AI infrastructure is becoming increasingly important to the US economy, and there is still a strong incentive to support investment in domestic computing capacity,” Knecht said.

For miners weighing a conversion, the question is whether AI revenue can justify the cost of upgrading cooling, networking and power systems. Brown thinks it can. “Miners will swap to AI because it is a better ROI than mining,” he said.

Clients must first get a license from NYSE to access the data through Pyth, the network said, noting that NYSE's data rules and agreements will continue to apply.

The data includes best bid and offer with size, trade prices, official closing prices, total trading volume, and alerts when trading is stopped or restarted, or short-sale restrictions apply. The feed covers NYSE, NYSE American, NYSE Arca, NYSE National and NYSE Texas. It also includes stocks and ETFs listed on other U.S. exchanges if they are traded on NYSE Group exchanges, Pyth said.

"As financial markets increasingly move onchain, the quality and integrity of the underlying data matter more than ever," Anthony Zawadzki, head of data and digital asset products at NYSE, said in a statement. He added that the collaboration gives builders and institutions another way to access NYSE data.

Pyth said platforms offering stock perpetual futures or tokenized shares can use the NYSE data to show users stock prices. NYSE provides data during market hours, while Pyth's own indices provide prices when markets are closed.

"Pyth Indices price U.S. equities 24/7. NYSE BQT carries the primary market close. Together, an app can show a user exactly how far a stock has moved since NYSE closed, through the night and over the weekend," the network said.

Pyth launched its data marketplace in April, with data providers including Euronext FX, Fidelity Investments, OTC Markets Group, SGX FX, Tradeweb and Exchange Data International.

The marketplace allows institutions to provide their data to other companies while deciding how much to charge, how their data is credited, and the terms for using it, according to Pyth.

#5105. Apex Group joins Hedera Council to explore tokenization and settlement

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

The Hedera partnership builds on Apex Group's existing work bringing blockchain infrastructure, stablecoins and staking products into traditional financial services.

Apex Group, a global financial services provider overseeing more than $3.5 trillion in assets, has joined the Hedera Council, bringing its expertise in fund administration, digital assets and institutional market infrastructure to the governance of the public blockchain network.

The company plans to explore using Hedera for its digital asset and tokenization initiatives, including asset lifecycle management, compliance and settlement, as institutional adoption of tokenized financial products expands.

"Institutional tokenization will scale only when compliance is embedded throughout the asset lifecycle, not added as an afterthought," said Marco Infuso, head of digital assets, Central Europe, at Apex Group. "That principle underpins our use of ERC-3643, the standard for compliant tokenization. By removing technological complexity, we can give clients a seamless experience and the flexibility to hold assets in traditional or tokenized form, with consistent standards of control and protection."

The Hedera partnership builds on Apex Group's existing work bringing blockchain infrastructure, stablecoins and staking products into traditional financial services.

Its Tokeny unit partnered with Polygon to build a blockchain for permissioned ERC-3643 tokens, with Apex Group serving as the initial onchain transfer agent. Separately, Apex partnered with World Liberty Financial to test USD1 stablecoin infrastructure in traditional fund administration, including subscriptions and redemptions for tokenized funds.

In 2024, Apex also played a role in launching institutional ETH and SOL staking exchange-traded products on the SIX Swiss Exchange.

"Apex Group combines deep expertise in private-market servicing with a clear vision for digital assets," said Mance Harmon, chair of the Hedera Council. "Its addition strengthens the Council at a pivotal moment, as institutional tokenization moves from experimentation to real-world adoption."

#5104. Kraken Parent Payward Brings 200 UK and EU Stocks Onchain as xStocks

Kraken Parent Payward Brings 200 UK and EU Stocks Onchain as xStocks

Payward, the parent company of crypto exchange Kraken, has tokenized more than 200 UK and European stocks through its xStocks platform, it announced on Wednesday.

The first batch covers some of the most actively traded companies listed in the UK and the European Union, with more to be added on a rolling basis. Like other xStocks, each token is backed 1:1 by the underlying share, which is bought and held by a regulated custodian for as long as the token trades, according to Payward.

Payward's @xStocksFi is expanding beyond US tokenized equities.

In partnership with @GTNglobal, more than 200 of the UK and EU’s largest equities are now tokenized by xStocks, including HSBC, Shell, LVMH and Airbus.

The first international launch, with more markets to follow.…

The tokens are available to trade on Kraken and through other platforms in the xStocks Alliance, and on blockchains where xStocks already trade, including Solana, Ethereum and TON. They are offered in more than 110 markets, but remain unavailable to investors in the UK.

"A portfolio should not have borders or trading hours," said Mark Greenberg, Payward's chief commercial officer. "Tokenizing every other international market is the next step."

The launch takes xStocks past 1,500 tokenized stocks, ETFs and IPOs. The platform holds more than $1.1 billion in assets, has processed over $45 billion in total transaction volume, and has more than 550,000 holders, Payward said.

The new tokens are the first delivered under Payward's partnership with GTN, a brokerage infrastructure firm that handles execution and custody of the underlying shares. When the two partnered in July, Payward said it planned to start with Hong Kong-listed stocks; hundreds of Hong Kong listings will now follow in the coming weeks, the company said.

The expansion also delivers on part of Payward's partnership with the London Stock Exchange, announced in September, under which Payward agreed to tokenize the 100 largest London-listed companies. Subject to regulatory approval, the exchange intends to list xStocks and begin trading them on LSE 24, its planned near-24-hour trading venue, in 2027.

Payward has been drawing interest from traditional exchanges. Nasdaq agreed to invest $100 million in the company at a $21 billion valuation in September, building on a March partnership to bring tokenized stocks to market in 2027, while Deutsche Börse bought a $200 million stake in April.

The company has also been expanding through acquisitions, agreeing to buy derivatives exchange Bitnomial for $550 million and Lithuania's Saldo Bank as part of a push into the EU.
